title: Choreography and Motion Mapping
answer: Kinematic generation, notation, motion capture retargeting, crowd simulation and biomechanics.

children.name: Kinematic Video and Generated Movement
children.blurb: Kinematic video and generated movement covers systems that read recorded human motion from video, estimate joint positions over time, and produce new movement sequences for dance, theatre, animation, or physical training.

children.name: Dance Notation and Transcription
children.blurb: Dance notation and transcription is the practice of recording human movement in symbolic or digital form so choreography can be preserved, analyzed, and restaged.

sections.body: This field applies machine learning to how bodies move, alone and in groups. Kinematic generation produces new movement sequences from learned patterns, while motion capture retargeting transfers recorded motion from one body or rig to another. Dance notation and transcription work on converting movement into readable scores or text, and crowd simulation models how many moving figures avoid collisions and form patterns. Biomechanical analysis measures forces, joint angles, and muscle activity to understand physical limits. In practice these systems are used in animation, game production, dance research, and rehabilitation, though the site currently tracks no live video models or AI tools in this area.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The work is uneven. Motion capture retargeting is mature for simple humanoid rigs, but retargeting to nonhuman bodies or handling complex contact with objects remains difficult. Generated movement often looks plausible in short clips but can drift, repeat, or lose physical grounding over longer sequences. Dance notation systems still require human correction because automatic transcription misreads subtle weight shifts and stylistic intent. Crowd simulation handles basic avoidance well, but realistic social behavior like turn taking or emotional response is not solved. Biomechanical analysis can measure motion accurately in controlled settings, yet it struggles with noisy real world video and individual variation.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: A reader interested in how new motion is created should start with Kinematic Video and Generated Movement, which explains the generative side. Dance Notation and Transcription connects that output to formal written scores and the limits of automatic reading. Motion Capture and Retargeting covers the pipeline from recorded performance to usable animation data, and it pairs naturally with Biomechanical Analysis for understanding the physical body behind the capture. Crowd and Ensemble Simulation extends the focus from one body to many, showing how individual motion rules scale into group behavior. Together these pages move from single generated clips to notation, capture, physical measurement, and finally large groups.
